It would be a simple matter for any one who has read my book to tell me what
are the two things which most people mistake and mix up with each other in
their mind. But the two questions which I believe them to be are these:

Firstly: “What is <GROUP>?”

Secondly: “What does it mean when they call a man <PERSON>?”

The distinction is very simple, if you only know how to think of it. We may
call a man a gentleman, because he is rich; we cannot call him a rich man,
because he is a gentleman. To have money means being wealthy; to be a good
man means having good qualities. The first thing which distinguishes an
<PLACE>, therefore, is his wealth. A man called by that name must either be
poor, like Mr. <PERSON>, or else a person of wealth and fortune like Mr.
<PERSON>. And then there remains the second question, “But what do we mean
by calling him rich?” And here again we find ourselves back at this same
difficult problem--the difference between mere riches and real wealth.

It is not the case that all gentlemen have money, just as it is not true
that all rich men have money. It is true, however, that every single man
who is really rich is a gentleman. The truth of the matter lies in this:
every rich man is certainly not a gentleman, unless he happens also to be
a man of some culture or education, a man of some refinement and taste, a
man of something finer than mere wealth. And if he were a gentleman,
he could never be poor. If he was poor, no amount of wealth would make him
rich. He might become rich, but not more than another man of less mental
culture than himself.

prompt: Write a meditation on an everyday household object, exploring its deeper significance through extended metaphor.

It is one of the things that I have always found curious about the modern
world. There seems to be something in it which does not fit together,
even by chance. A man may live in a country town without knowing why he
is there; but when he has come into this <ORG> city he suddenly
feels as if he was wandering in some strange place--strange even from
the point of view of the country towns.

That the old houses are out of place I am quite sure. It is like seeing
a man in his own coat while going to dinner at somebody else’s house.
But it is equally absurd to say that the new buildings are out of place;
they seem to be more out of place than anything else in existence. This
odd feeling came upon me recently with regard to some chairs. For
example, every room must surely be made much more cheerful if you can
have a pair of chairs standing in the middle of it. And yet I cannot
think where they would be most noticeable. They might stand between two
doors facing each other, or opposite the chimney-piece. But it seemed
to me impossible for them to stand beside a fire-place. The chair would
appear to be too small and inconsequential to take any part whatever in
such an important thing as warmth and comfort. The fire-place, whether
in the kitchen or drawing-room, ought to look very large indeed when
it is warm. The chair ought to look very small and insignificant when
it is cold.
